messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan sits perfectly still in the chair, his back straight, not touching the cushion behind him. At thirty-six, he has the tired eyes of a much older man, a constant watchfulness that seems at odds with the quiet precision of his work as an accountant. He explains that his body feels like a tightly wound spring, and has for as long as he can remember. He is always prepared for a danger he cannot name, a posture of readiness that has become his natural state. His muscles ache with a tension that never subsides, a low-level hum of alertness that scans every room for exits and every new person for potential threats.

The memories, when they come, are not stories. Rohan lacks the words to assemble the events of his childhood into a coherent narrative. Instead, they are sensory assaults. Sometimes, it’s the memory of a sound: a dull, percussive thud against a wall, followed by a muffled sob. Other times, it’s a fleeting image: the pattern of the floral wallpaper in the hallway of his childhood home, viewed from a crack in his bedroom door. There is no beginning or end, only these terrifying fragments that ambush him without warning. He explains that when these moments hit, the terror is not a recollection; it is immediate and absolute, the same paralyzing fear a small boy felt hiding in his room, certain that making a single sound would draw the monster’s attention.

These ambushes have become more frequent. Last month, during a stressful quarter-end at his accounting firm, his manager dropped a heavy stack of files onto a metal cabinet. The sudden, sharp bang ricocheted through the quiet office. For everyone else, it was a startling noise. For Rohan, it was a detonation. His heart instantly began to hammer against his ribs, a cold sweat breaking out across his forehead. He felt the air leave his lungs, his vision tunneling as the fluorescent office lights seemed to flicker and dim. He was no longer a 36-year-old accountant in a downtown office; he was a child again, frozen and helpless, the echo of that thud against the wall vibrating through his entire body. He couldn’t speak, couldn’t move, until a colleague touched his arm, breaking the spell. He spent the next hour in the bathroom, unable to explain the visceral panic that had seized him.

Over the years, this internal state of siege has eroded his life from the inside out. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally incapable of stopping bad things from happening. This sense of helplessness is a constant companion, whispering that any moment of peace is merely a prelude to disaster. His father, the source of those terrifying sounds, was never held accountable. He moved on, remarried, and lives a comfortable life, a fact that cements Rohan’s conviction that the world is an unjust place where perpetrators walk free and the innocent are left to carry the wounds. This belief has poisoned his capacity for joy. He remembers being a younger man, before his marriage ended, who could laugh without reservation. Now, that person feels like a stranger. He looks at old photos and feels a profound sense of loss for the happiness he is certain he can never reclaim.

His ex-wife used to say it was like living with a ghost. He was physically present, but his mind was always somewhere else, cataloging potential dangers, his body rigid with a tension she could never soothe. The divorce felt less like a failure and more like an inevitability, another bad thing he was powerless to prevent. He sought help after the incident at work, terrified of losing the last pillar of stability in his life. He is afraid he is permanently damaged, that the alert, miserable man he is now is all that is left. His greatest hope is simply to feel safe inside his own skin, to convince his body that the war it has been fighting for three decades is finally over.
